extracted.intended_audience: mathematics education researchers, college calculus instructors, and undergraduate math educators
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of instructor and student discourse about the limit notation in beginning-level undergraduate calculus, including coding word use as objectified vs operational and examining how notation functions as a visual mediator. Also included are related conference reports on IBL outcomes and example-space analyses for probability-zero events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Units of analysis: word use and limit notation
rubrics_metrics.description: The units of analyses were the instructor's and students' word use, and the limit notation as a visual mediator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transcripts included speech and coded participant actions referring to the limit notation; analysis focused on how word use and the symbolic notation combine to produce realizations of limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectified versus operational word use
rubrics_metrics.description: Word use on limits was considered objectified if the participants talked about limit as an end-state or a number; it was considered operational if participants talked about limit as a process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this binary coding when analyzing discourse: objectification = talk about a limit as an end-state/number; operational = talk about a limiting process. Pay attention to contexts where instructors shift between these modes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention to metaphors and endorsed narratives
rubrics_metrics.description: Particular attention was given to the use of metaphors and endorsed narratives underlying participants' word use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the metaphors (e.g., continuous motion vs discreteness) and narratives (e.g., 'limit is a process' vs 'limit is a number') that participants rely on and whether those narratives are endorsed by students or instructor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual coding of limit talk
rubrics_metrics.description: The instructor's word use on the limit notation depended on three mathematical contexts: computing limit at a point; limit at infinity; and infinite limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When coding or interpreting discourse, separate analyses by these contexts because objectification/operationalization tendencies differ across them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of limit notation as mediator
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus on the limit notation as a symbolic representational tool in the discourse of limits since, besides graphing, it is the main visual mediator with which ideas about limit are communicated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine how the symbolic form (e.g., lim_{x→a} f(x) = L) can support either processual (dynamic motion) or objectified (end-result) realizations, and how that interacts with instruction and student sense-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicitness in instruction about underlying metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: The tacit nature of metaphors and students' adoption of the instructor's operational word use as dominant signals the importance of explicitness during instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation: instructors should make metaphors and discursive layers explicit to help students distinguish conceptual vs procedural aspects of limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data collection sources for discourse study
rubrics_metrics.description: For the instructor's discourse, data consisted of video-taped classroom observations and field notes; for students, data included responses to a diagnostic survey and task-based interviews (written work, audio-tape, field notes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect multiple data sources (video, audio, surveys, written work) to triangulate discourse patterns and referent actions; ensure voluntary participation and document durations of interviews/observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transcript coding includes actions and references to notation
rubrics_metrics.description: The transcripts for the video and audio-taped sessions included what the participants said and what they did; transcripts also coded participants' actions as they were referring to the limit notation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing transcripts for analysis, include embodied actions (gesture, pointing) and referent manipulations of notation, not just verbal utterances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure cognitive outcomes via multiple indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Cognitive outcomes were measured by self-reported learning gains from surveys, academic achievement measures from transcripts, and test data from a subset of courses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use converging measures (surveys, transcript grade data, pre/post tests) to assess cognitive gains rather than relying on a single instrument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define affective outcomes and proxies
rubrics_metrics.description: Affective outcomes included self-reported affective changes (pre/post survey items) and pursuit of additional mathematics courses used as a proxy for increased interest in mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include both attitudinal survey items and behavioral proxies (e.g., subsequent course-taking) when measuring affective outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survey instrument and scaling conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre- and post-surveys were used: Likert items (seven-point) for beliefs and pre/post gains measured on a five-point SALG scale from 'no gain' to 'great gains'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow established instruments (e.g., SALG) and report the scale anchors; ensure composite variables are constructed transparently from item responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of composite variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Composite variables were constructed on the basis of the designed scales, exploratory factor analyses, and item analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting composite measures, document scale design, factor analysis results, item reliabilities, and how items map into composites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of historical transcript data for longitudinal outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical transcript data included courses taken, grades obtained, majors/minors, and backgrounds (by term) and were used to examine post-course outcomes such as number of additional math courses taken and average grades.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use longitudinal academic records to assess durability of course effects (e.g., later course grades, continued enrollment in mathematics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical analysis conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Results are based on statistical analysis including descriptive statistics and parametric or non-parametric tests; differences reported as statistically significant (example p<.001).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report choice of statistical tests, assumptions checked, effect sizes and significance levels; explicitly state significance thresholds and whether tests are parametric or non-parametric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subgroup analysis by gender and prior achievement
rubrics_metrics.description: Break out student outcomes by gender and prior achievement levels (e.g., GPA tertiles) to examine differential effects — e.g., IBL benefits particularly evident for women and lower-achieving students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-specify subgroup boundaries (GPA thresholds) and ensure sample sizes are adequate for subgroup inference; interpret subgroup findings cautiously when sample sizes are small.

rubrics_metrics.name: GPA-based grouping heuristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Groups divided by self-reported college GPA into rough thirds: top (!3.8 or >3.4 in another campus example), high (3.0-3.79 or 2.5-3.4), and moderate/low (<3.0 or <2.5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing by prior achievement, clearly state cutoffs used and justify them; different campuses/projects may use slightly different thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of pre/post tests to corroborate survey findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre/post tests (e.g., mathematical knowledge for teaching) provided corroborating evidence, showing largest gains among students who scored lowest on the pre-test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include objective pre/post testing where feasible and analyze differential gains by initial proficiency to detect where instruction helps most.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of probability-zero example types
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of probability-zero events were categorized by participants into types such as 'zero divided by a non-zero' (called 'logically impossible' events), and other categories based on how a fraction could be equal to zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When studying example spaces, code and report the classification scheme (categories, examples per category) and tie categories back to formal probability definitions (classical vs measure-theoretic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Example-space perspective for concept understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: A concept is awareness of dimensions of possible variation; example space is the collection of permissible variations — tasks asking learners to construct examples both extend their example space and reveal sophistication of conceptual awareness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design tasks that elicit participants' example space (e.g., 'give an example of an event with probability zero' and a 'more complicated' example) and analyze the range and types of examples produced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research ethics and participation notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Participation in the survey and the task-based interviews was voluntary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document voluntary consent, and when using surveys/interviews ensure participants understand voluntary nature and any confidentiality protections.
